gabardine.etymology: Sp. gabardina; cf. It. gavardina, OF. galvardine, calvardine, gavardine, galeverdine; perh. akin to Sp. & OF. gaban a sort of cloak or coat for rainy weather, F. caban great coat with a hood and sleeves, It. gabbano and perh. to E. cabin.

gabble.etymology: Freq. of gab. See Gab, v. i.

gaberdine.etymology: Sp. gabardina; cf. It. gavardina, OF. galvardine, calvardine, gavardine, galeverdine; perh. akin to Sp. & OF. gaban a sort of cloak or coat for rainy weather, F. caban great coat with a hood and sleeves, It. gabbano and perh. to E. cabin.

gable.etymology: OE. gable, gabil, F. gable, fr. LL. gabalum front of a building, prob. of German or Scand. origin; cf. OHG. gibil, G. giebel gable, Icel. gafl, Goth. gibla pinnacle; perh. akin to Gr. cephalic, or to G. gabel fork, AS. geafl, E. gaffle, L. gabalus a kind of gallows.

gad.etymology: OE. gad, Icel. gaddr goad, sting; akin to Sw. gadd sting, Goth. gazds, G. gerte switch. See Yard a measure.

gadoid.etymology: NL. gadus cod + -oid: cf. F. gadoïde gadoid, Gr. gade.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

gadolinite.etymology: Named after Gadolin, a Russian chemist.

gaelic.etymology: Gael. Gàidhealach, Gaelach, from Gàidheal, Gael, a Scotch Highlander.

gaff.etymology: OE. gaffe, F. gaffe an iron hook with which seamen pull great fishes into their ships; cf. Ir. gaf, gafa hook; perh. akin to G. gabel fork, Skr. gabhasti. CF. Gaffle, Gable.

gaffer.etymology: Possibly contr. fr. godfather; but prob. fr. gramfer for grandfather. Cf. Gammer.

gag.etymology: Prob. fr. W. cegio to choke or strangle, fr. ceg mouth, opening, entrance.

gage.etymology: F. gage, LL. gadium, wadium; of German origin; cf. Goth. wadi, OHG. wetti, weti, akin to E. wed. See Wed, and cf. Wage, n.

gaggle.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. D. gaggelen, gagelen, G. gackeln, gackern, MHG. g, E. giggle, cackle.

gainsay.etymology: OE. geinseien, ageinseien. See Again, and Say to utter.

gaiter.etymology: F. guêtre, cf. Armor. gweltren; or perh. of German origin, and akin to E. wear, v.

gala.etymology: F. gala show, pomp, fr. It. gala finery, gala; of German origin. See Gallant.

galangal.etymology: OE. galingale, OF. galingal, garingal, F. galanga (cf. Sp. galanga), prob. fr. Ar. khalanj.

galaxy.etymology: F. galaxie, L. galaxias, fr. Gr. lac. CF. Lacteal.

galbanum.etymology: L. galbanum, Gr. klekb'n: cf. F. galbanum.

gale.etymology: Prob. of Scand.. origin; cf. Dan. gal furious, Icel. galinn, cf. Icel. gala to sing, AS. galan to sing, Icel. galdr song, witchcraft, AS. galdor charm, sorcery, E. nightingale; also, Icel. gjla gust of wind, gola breeze. Cf. Yell.

galena.etymology: L. galena lead ore, dross that remains after melting lead: cf. F. galène sulphide of lead ore, antidote to prison, stillness of the sea, calm, tranquility.

galician.etymology: Cf. Sp. Galiciano, Gallego, fr. L. Gallaecus, Gallaicus, fr. Gallaeci a people in Western Spain.

galilean.etymology: L. Galilaeus, fr. Galilaea Galilee, Gr. galiléen.

galilee.etymology: Supposed to have been so termed in allusion to the scriptural "Galilee of the Gentiles." cf. OF. galilée.

gall.etymology: OE. galle, gal, AS. gealla; akin to D. gal, OS. & OHG. galla, Icel. gall, SW. galla, Dan. galde, L. fel, Gr. yellow. Yellow, and cf. Choler

gallant.etymology: F. gallant, prop. p. pr. of OF. galer to rejoice, akin to OF. gale amusement, It. gala ornament; of German origin; cf. OHG. geil merry, luxuriant, wanton, G. geil lascivious, akin to AS. g wanton, wicked, OS. g merry, Goth. gailjan to make to rejoice, or perh. akin to E. weal. See Gala, Galloon.

galleon.etymology: Sp. galeon, cf. F. galion; fr. LL. galeo, galio. See Galley.

gallery.etymology: F. galerie, It. galleria, fr. LL. galeria gallery, perh. orig., a festal hall, banquetting hall; cf. OF. galerie a rejoicing, fr. galer to rejoice. Cf. Gallant, a.

gallimaufry.etymology: F. galimafrée a sort of ragout or mixed hash of different meats.

gallinaceous.etymology: L. gallinaceus, fr. gallina hen, fr. gallus cock.

gallinule.etymology: L. gallinula chicken, dim. of gallina hen: cf. F. gallinule.

gallon.etymology: OF galon, jalon, LL. galo, galona, fr. galum a liquid measure; cf. F. jale large bowl. Cf. Gill a measure.

gallop.etymology: OE. galopen, F. galoper, of German origin; cf. assumed Goth. ga-hlaupan to run, OHG. giloufen, AS. gehleápan to leap, dance, fr. root of E. leap, and a prefix; or cf. OFlem. walop a gallop. See Leap, and cf. 1st Wallop.

gallows.etymology: OE. galwes, pl., AS. galga, gealga, gallows, cross; akin to D. galg gallows, OS. & OHG. galgo, G. galgen, Icel. galgi, Sw. & Dan. galge, Goth. galga a cross. Etymologically and historically considered, gallows is a noun in the plural number, but it is used as a singular, and hence is preceded by a; as, a gallows.

galore.etymology: Scot. gelore, gilore, galore, fr. Gael. gu leòr, enough; gu- to, also an adverbial prefix + leòr, leòir, enough; or fr. Ir. goleor, the same word.

galvanic.etymology: From Galvani, a professor of physiology at Bologna, on account of his connection (about 1780) with the discovery of dynamical or current electricity: cf. F. galvanique.

galvanism.etymology: From Galvani: cf. F. galvanisme. See Galvanic.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

gambit.etymology: F. gambit, cf. It. gambitto gambit, a tripping up. See Gambol, n.

gambol.etymology: OE. gambolde, gambaulde, F. gambade, gambol, fr. It. gambata kick, fr. L. gamba leg, akin to F. jambe, OF. also, gambe, fr. L. gamba, hoof or perh. joint: cf. Gr. cam crooked; perh. akin to E. chamber: cf.F. gambiller to kick about. Cf. Jamb, n., Gammon ham, Gambadoes.

gambrel.etymology: OF. gambe, jambe leg, F. jambe. Cf. Cambrel, Chambrel, and see Gambol. n.

game.etymology: Cf. W. cam crooked, and E. gambol, n.

gamete.etymology: Gr. gameth` wife, or game`ths husband, fr. gamei^n to marry.

gammon.etymology: OF. gambon, F. jambon, fr. OF. gambe leg, F. jambe. See Gambol, n., and cf. Ham.

gamut.etymology: F. gamme + ut the name of a musical note. F. gamme is fr. the name of the Greek letter Gamma, and Ut.

gander.etymology: AS. gandra, ganra, akin to Prov. G. gander, ganter, and E. goose, gannet. See Goose.

gang.etymology: AS. gangan, akin to OS. & OHG. gangan, Icel. ganga, Goth. gaggan; cf. Lith. to walk, Skr. ja leg. sq. root48. CF. Go.

ganglion.etymology: L. ganglion a sort of swelling or excrescence, a tumor under the skin, Gr. ganglion.

gangrene.etymology: F. gangrène, L. gangraena, fr. Gr. gras, gar, to devour, and E. voracious, also canker, n., in sense 3.

gannet.etymology: OE. gant, AS. ganet, ganot, a sea fowl, a fen duck; akin to D. gent gander, OHG. ganazzo. See Gander, Goose.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

gap.etymology: OE. gap; cf. Icel. gap an empty space, Sw. gap mouth, breach, abyss, Dan. gab mouth, opening, AS. geap expanse; as adj., wide, spacious. See Gape.

gape.etymology: OE. gapen, AS. geapan to open; akin to D. gapen to gape, G. gaffen, Icel. & Sw. gapa, Dan. gabe; cf. Skr. jabh to snap at, open the mouth. Cf. Gaby, Gap.

gar.etymology: Prob. AS. gar dart, spear, lance. The name is applied to the fish on account of its long and slender body and pointed head. Cf. Goad, Gore, v.

garb.etymology: OF. garbe looks, countenance, grace, ornament, fr. OHG. garawi, garwi, ornament, dress. akin to E. gear. See Gear, n.

garbage.etymology: OE. also garbash, perh. orig., that which is purged or cleansed away; cf. OF. garber to make fine, neat, OHG. garawan to make ready, prepare, akin to E. garb dress; or perh. for garbleage, fr. garble; or cf. OF. garbage tax on sheaves, E. garb sheaf.

garble.etymology: Formerly, to pick out, sort, OF. grabeler, for garbeler to examine precisely, garble spices, fr. LL. garbellare to sift; cf. Sp. garbillar to sift, garbillo a coarse sieve, L. cribellum, dim. of cribrum sieve, akin to cernere to separate, sift (cf. E. Discern); or perh. rather from Ar. gharbal, gharbil, sieve.

garboil.etymology: OF. garbouil; cf. Sp. garbullo, It. garbuglio; of uncertain origin; the last part is perh. fr. L. bullire to boil, E. boil.

garden.etymology: OE. gardin, OF. gardin, jardin, F. jardin, of German origin; cf. OHG. garto, G. garten; akin to AS. geard. See Yard an inclosure.

gargantuan.etymology: From Gargantua, an allegorical hero of Rabelais.

garget.etymology: OE. garget, gargate, throat, OF. gargate. Cf. Gorge. The etymol. of senses 2, 3, & 4 is not certain.

gargle.etymology: F. gargouiller to dabble, paddle, gargle. Cf. Gargoyle, Gurgle.

gargoyle.etymology: OE. garguilie, gargouille, cf. Sp. gárgola, prob. fr. the same source as F. gorge throat, influenced by L. gargarizare to gargle. See Gorge and cf. Gargle, Gargarize.

garish.etymology: Cf. OE. gauren to stare; of uncertain origin. Cf. gairish.

garland.etymology: OE. garland, gerlond, OF. garlande, F. guirlande; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. wiara, wiera, crown, pure gold, MHG. wieren to adorn.

garlic.etymology: OE. garlek, AS. garleác; gar spear, lance + leác leek. See Gar, n., and Leek.

garment.etymology: OE. garnement, OF. garnement, garniment, fr. garnir to garnish. See Garnish.

garner.etymology: OE. garner, gerner, greiner, OF. gernier, grenier, F. grenier, fr. L. granarium, fr. granum. See 1st Grain, and cf. Granary.

garnet.etymology: OE. gernet, grenat, OF. grenet,grenat, F. grenat, LL. granatus, fr. L. granatum pomegranate, granatus having many grains or seeds, fr. granum grain, seed. So called from its resemblance in color and shape to the grains or seeds of the pomegranate. See Grain, and cf. Grenade, Pomegranate.

garnierite.etymology: Named after the French geologist Garnier.

garnish.etymology: OE. garnischen, garnissen, OF. garnir to provide, strengthen, prepare, garnish, warn, F. garnir to provide, furnish, garnish, -- of German origin; cf. OHG. warnon to provide, equip; akin to G. wahren to watch, E. aware, ware, wary, and cf. also E. warn. See Wary, -ish, and cf. Garment, Garrison.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

garnishment.etymology: Cf. OF. garnissement protection, guarantee, warning.

garret.etymology: OE. garite, garette, watchtower, place of lookout, OF. garite, also meaning, a place of refuge, F. guérite a place of refuge, donjon, sentinel box, fr. OF. garir to preserve, save, defend, F. guérir to cure; of German origin; cf. OHG. werian to protect, defend, hinder, G. wehren, akin to Goth. warjan to hinder, and akin to E. weir, or perhaps to wary. See Weir, and cf. Guerite.

garrison.etymology: OE. garnisoun, F. garnison garrison, in OF. & OE. also, provision, munitions, from garnir to garnish. See Garnish.

garrote.etymology: Sp. garrote, from garra claw, talon, of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. & W. gar leg, ham, shank. Cf. Garrot stick, Garter.

garrulous.etymology: L. garrulus, fr. garrire to chatter, talk; cf. Gr. Call.

garter.etymology: OE. gartier, F. jarretière, fr. OF. garet bend of the knee, F. jarret; akin to Sp. garra claw, Prov. garra leg. See Garrote.

gas.etymology: Invented by the chemist Van Helmont of Brussels, who died in 1644.

gasconade.etymology: F. gasconnade, from Gascon an inhabitant of Gascony, the people of which were noted for boasting.

gash.etymology: For older garth or garse, OF. garser to scarify, F. gercer to chap, perh. from an assumed LL. carptiare, fr. L. carpere, carptum, to pluck, separate into parts; cf. LL. carptare to wound. Cf. Carpet.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

gasket.etymology: Cf. F. garcette, It. gaschetta, Sp. cajeta caburn, garceta reef point.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

gasp.etymology: OE. gaspen, gaispen, to yawn, gasp, Icel. geispa to yawn; akin to Sw. gäspa, Dan. gispe to gasp.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
A combining form from the Gr. gastrocolic, gastrocele, gastrotomy.

A combining form from the Gr. gastrocolic, gastrocele, gastrotomy.
A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.
A combining form from the Gr. gastrocolic, gastrocele, gastrotomy.
A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

gate.etymology: OE. et, , giat, gate, door, AS. geat, gat, gate, door; akin to OS., D., & Icel. gat opening, hole, and perh. to E. gate a way, gait, and get, v. Cf. Gate a way in the wall, 3d Get.

gather.etymology: OE. gaderen, AS. gaderian, gadrian, fr. gador, geador, together, fr. gæd fellowship; akin to E. good, D. gaderen to collect, G. gatte husband, MHG. gate, also companion, Goth. gadiliggs a sister's son. sq. root29. See Good, and cf. Together.

gaud.etymology: OE. gaude jest, trick, gaudi bead of a rosary, fr. L. gaudium joy, gladness. See Joy.

gauffer.etymology: F. gaufrer to figure cloth, velvet, and other stuffs, fr. gaufre honeycomb, waffle; of German origin. See Waffle, Wafer, and cf. Goffer, Gopher an animal.

gauge.etymology: OF. gaugier, F. jauger, cf. OF. gauge gauge, measuring rod, F. jauge; of uncertain origin; perh. fr. an assumed L. qualificare to determine the qualities of a thing (see Qualify); but cf. also F. jalon a measuring stake in surveying, and E. gallon.

gaul.etymology: F. Gaule, fr. L. Gallia, fr. Gallus a Gaul.

gaunt.etymology: Cf. Norw. gand a thin pointed stick, a tall and thin man, and W. gwan weak.

gauntlet.etymology: F. gantelet, dim. of gant glove, LL. wantus, of Teutonic origin; cf. D. want, Sw. & Dan. vante, Icel. vöttr, for vantr.

gauntry.etymology: F. chantier, LL. cantarium, fr. L. canterius trellis, sort of frame.

gauze.etymology: F. gaze; so called because it was first introduced from Gaza, a city of Palestine.

gavel.etymology: OF. gavelle, F. javelle, prob. dim. from L. capulus handle, fr. capere to lay hold of, seize; or cf. W. gafael hold, grasp. Cf. Heave.

gawk.etymology: OE. gok, gowk, cuckoo, fool, Icel. gaukr cuckoo; akin to OHG. gouh, G. gauch cuckoo, fool, AS. géac cuckoo, Sw. gök, Dan. giög

gay.etymology: F. gai, perhaps fr. OHG. g swift, rapid, G. gäh, jäh, steep, hasty; or cf. OHG. w beatiful, good. Cf. Jay.

gaze.etymology: OE. gasen, akin to dial. Sw. gasa, cf. Goth. us-gaisjan to terrify, us- geisnan to be terrified. Cf. Aghast, Ghastly, Ghost, Hesitate.

gazelle.etymology: F. gazelle, OF. also, gazel; cf. Sp. gacela, Pr. gazella, It. gazella; all fr. Ar. ghaz a wild goat.

gazette.etymology: F. gazette, It. gazzetta, perh. from gazetta a Venetian coin (see Gazet), said to have been the price of the first newspaper published at Venice; or perh. dim. of gazza magpie, a name perh. applied to the first newspaper; cf. OHG. agalstra magpie, G. elster.

gean.etymology: F. guigne the fruit of the gean; cf. OHG. wihsila, G. weichsel.

gear.etymology: OE. gere, ger, AS. gearwe clothing, adornment, armor, fr. gearo, gearu, ready, yare; akin to OHG. garawi, garwi ornament, dress. See Yare, and cf. Garb dress.

gecko.etymology: Cf. F. & G. gecko; -- so called from the sound which the animal utters.

geld.etymology: AS. gild, gield, geld, tribute, payment, fr. gieldan to pay, render. See Yield.

gelding.etymology: Icel. gelding a gelding, akin to geldingr wether, eunuch, Sw. gälling gelding, Dan. gilding eunuch. See Geld, v. t.

gelid.etymology: L. gelidus, fr. gelun frost, cold. See Cold, and cf. Congeal, Gelatin, Jelly.

gem.etymology: OE. gemme precious stone, F. gemme, fr. L. gemma a precious stone, bud.

geminate.etymology: L. geminatus, p.p. of genimare to double. See Gemini.

gemini.etymology: L., twins, pl. of geminus; cf. Skr. j related as brother or sister.

gemmiferous.etymology: L. gemma bud + -ferous: cf. F. gemmifère.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

gemmule.etymology: L. gemmula, dim. of gemma: cf. F. gemmule. See Gem.

gemsbok.etymology: D.; akin to G. gemsbock the male or buck of the chamois; gemse chamois, goat of the Alps + bock buck.

gender.etymology: OF. genre, gendre (with excrescent d.), F.genre, fr. L. genus, generis, birth, descent, race, kind, gender, fr. the root of genere, gignere, to beget, in pass., to be born, akin to E. kin. See Kin, and cf. Generate, Genre, Gentle, Genus.

general.etymology: F. général, fr. L. generalis. See Genus.

generalissimo.etymology: It., superl. of generale general. See General, a.

generality.etymology: L. generalitas: cf. F. généralité. Cf. Generalty.

generate.etymology: L. generatus, p. p. of generare to generate, fr. genus. See Genus, Gender.

generation.etymology: OE. generacioun, F. génération, fr.L. generatio.

generic.etymology: L. genus, generis, race, kind: cf. F. générique. See Gender.

generous.etymology: F. généreux, fr. L. generous of noble birth, noble, excellent, magnanimous, fr. genus birth, race: cf. It. generoso. See 2d Gender.

genesis.etymology: L., from Gr. genus birth, race. See Gender.

geneva.etymology: F. genièvre juniper, juniper berry, gin, OF. geneivre juniper, fr. L. juniperus the juniper tree: cf. D. jenever, fr. F. genièvre. See Juniper, and cf. Gin a liquor.

genial.etymology: L. genialis: cf. OF. genial. See Genius.

geniculate.etymology: L. geniculatus, fr. geniculum little knee, knot or joint, dim. of genu knee. See Knee.

genital.etymology: L. genitalis, fr. genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. génital. See Gender.

genitals.etymology: From Genital, a.: cf. L. genitalia.

genitive.etymology: L. genitivus, fr. gignere, genitum, to beget: cf. F. génitif. See Gender.

genius.etymology: L. genius, prop., the superior or divine nature which is innate in everything, the spirit, the tutelar deity or genius of a person or place, taste, talent, genius, from genere, gignere, to beget, bring forth. See Gender, and cf. Engine.

gent.etymology: OF. gent, fr. L. genitus born, or (less prob.) fr. gentilis. See Genteel.

genteel.etymology: F. gentil noble, pretty, graceful. See Gentle.

gentian.etymology: OE. genciane, F. gentiane, L. gentiana, fr. Gentius, an Illyrian king, said to have discovered its properties.

gentile.etymology: L. gentilis belonging to the same clan, stock, race, people, or nation; in opposition to Roman, a foreigner; in opposition to Jew or Christian, a heathen: cf. F. gentil. See Gentle, a.

gentility.etymology: L. gentilitas the relationship of those who belong to the same clan, also, heathenism: cf. F. gentilité heathenism. See Gentile.

gentle.etymology: OE. gentil, F. gentil noble, pretty, graceful, fr. L. gentilis of the same clan or race, fr. gens, gentis, tribe, clan, race, orig. that which belongs together by birth, fr. the root of genere, gignere, to beget; hence gentle, properly, of birth or family, that is, of good or noble birth. See Gender, and cf. Genteel, Gentil, Gentile, Gentoo, Jaunty.

gentleman.etymology: OE. gentilman nobleman; gentil noble + man man; cf. F. gentilhomme.

gentry.etymology: OE. genterie, gentrie, noble birth, nobility, cf. gentrise, and OF. gentelise, genterise, E. gentilesse, also OE. genteleri high-mindedness. See Gent, a., Gentle, a.

genuflection.etymology: F. génuflexion, fr. LL. genuflexio, fr. L. genu knee + flexio a bending, fr. flectere, flexum, to bend. See Knee, Flexible.

genuine.etymology: L. genuinus, fr. genere, gignere, to beget, in pass., to be born: cf. F. génuine. See Gender.

genus.etymology: L., birth, race, kind, sort; akin to Gr. Gender, and cf. Benign.

geochemistry.etymology: Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth + chemistry.

geography.etymology: F. géographie, l. geographia, fr. Gr. Graphic.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

geometer.etymology: F. géomètre, L. geometres, geometra, fr. Gr. Meter measure.

geometry.etymology: F. géométrie, L. geometria, fr. Gr. Geometer.

george.etymology: F. George, or Georges, a proper name, fr. Gr. work. See Work.

geranium.etymology: L., fr. Gr. géranium. See Crane, n.

germ.etymology: F. germe, fr. L. germen, germinis, sprout, but, germ. Cf. Germen, Germane.

german.etymology: OE. german, germain, F. germain, fr. L. germanus full, own (said of brothers and sisters who have the same parents); akin to germen germ. Cf. Germ, Germane.

germander.etymology: OE. germaunder, F. germandrée, It. calamandrea, L. chamaedrys, fr. Gr.Humble, and Tree.

germanic.etymology: L. Germanicus: cf. F. germanique. See German, n.

germinate.etymology: L. germinatus, p. p. of germinare to sprout, fr. germen. See Germ.

gerund.etymology: L. gerundium, fr. gerere to bear, carry, perform. See Gest a deed, Jest.

gestation.etymology: L. gestatio a bearing, carrying, fr. gestare to bear, carry, intens. fr. gerere, gestum, to bear: cf. F. gestation. See Gest deed, Jest.

gesticulate.etymology: L. gesticulatus, p. p. of gesticulari to gesticulate, fr. gesticulus a mimic gesture, gesticulation, dim. of gestus gesture, fr. gerere, gestum, to bear, carry, peform. See Gestic.

gesture.etymology: LL. gestura mode of action, fr. L. gerere, gestum, to bear, behave, perform, act. See Gest a deed.

gewgaw.etymology: OE. gigawe, gugawe, gewgaude, prob. the same word as OE. givegove gewgaw, apparently a reduplicated form fr. AS. gifan to give; cf. also F. joujou plaything, and E. gaud, n. See Give, and cf. Giffgaff.

geyser.etymology: Icel. geysir, fr. geysa to rush furiously, fr. gj to gush. Cf. Gush.

ghastly.etymology: OE. gastlich, gastli, fearful, causing fear, fr. gasten to terrify, AS. gæstan. Cf. Aghast, Gast, Gaze, Ghostly.

ghee.etymology: Hind. ghi clarified butter, Skr. gh.

gherkin.etymology: D. agurkje, a dim. akin to G. gurke, Dan. ag; cf. Pol. ogórek, Bohem. okurka, LGr. al-khiyar, Per. khiyar.

ghost.etymology: OE. gast, gost, soul, spirit, AS. gast breath, spirit, soul; akin to OS. g spirit, soul, D. geest, G. geist, and prob. to E. gaze, ghastly.

ghostly.etymology: OE. gastlich, gostlich, AS. gastlic. See Ghost.

ghoul.etymology: Per. gh an imaginary sylvan demon, supposed to devour men and animals: cf. Ar. gh, F. goule.

giant.etymology: OE. giant, geant, geaunt, OF. jaiant, geant, F. géant, L. gigas, fr. Gr. gender, genesis. See Gender, and cf. Gigantic.

gib.etymology: Abbreviated fr. Gilbert, the name of the cat in the old story of "Reynard the Fox". in the "Romaunt of the Rose", etc.

gibbet.etymology: OE. gibet, F. gibet, in OF. also club, fr. LL. gibetum;; cf. OF. gibe sort of sickle or hook, It. giubbetto gibbet, and giubbetta, dim. of giubba mane, also, an under waistcoat, doublet, Prov. It. gibba (cf. Jupon); so that it perhaps originally signified a halter, a rope round the neck of malefactors; or it is, perhaps, derived fr. L. gibbus hunched, humped, E. gibbous; or cf. E. jib a sail.

gibbose.etymology: L. gibbosus, fr. gibbus, gibba, hunch, hump. Cf. Gibbous.

gibe.etymology: Cf. Prov. F. giber, equiv. to F. jouer to play, Icel. geipa to talk nonsense, E. jabber.

giblets.etymology: OE. gibelet, OF. gibelet game: cf. F. gibelotte stewed rabbit. Cf. Gibbier.

giddy.etymology: OE. gidi mad, silly, AS. gidig, of unknown origin, cf. Norw. gidda to shake, tremble.

gift.etymology: OE. gift, yift, yeft, AS. gift, fr. gifan to give; akin to D. & G. gift, Icel. gift, gipt, Goth. gifts (in comp.). See Give, v. t.

gig.etymology: Cf. OF. gigue. See Jig, n.

giggle.etymology: Akin to gaggle: cf. OD. ghichelen, G. kichern.

gigot.etymology: F., fr. OF. gigue fiddle; -- on account of the resemblance in shape. See Jig, n.

gild.etymology: AS. gyldan, from gold gold. sq. root234. See Gold.

gill.etymology: Dan. giælle, gelle; akin to Sw. gäl, Icel. gjölnar gills; cf. AS. geagl, geahl, jaw.

gillyflower.etymology: OE. gilofre, gilofer, clove, OF. girofre, girofle, F. girofle: cf. F. giroflée gillyflower, fr. girofle, Gr. foliage. Cf. Caryophyllus, July-flower.

gimcrack.etymology: OE., a spruce and pert pretender, also, a spruce girl, prob. fr. gim + crack lad, boaster.

gimlet.etymology: OF. guimbelet, guibelet, F. gibelet, prob. fr. OD. wimpel, weme, a bore, wemelen to bore, to wimble. See Wimble, n.

ginger.etymology: OE. ginger, gingever, gingivere, OF. gengibre, gingimbre, F. gingembre, L. zingiber, zingiberi, fr. Gr. zenjebil, fr. Skr. , prop., hornshaped; horn + vëra body.

gingerly.etymology: Prov. E. ginger brittle, tender; cf. dial. Sw. gingla, gängla, to go gently, totter, akin to E. gang.

gingham.etymology: F. guingan; cf. Jav. ginggang; or perh. fr. Guingamp, in France.

giraffe.etymology: F. girafe, Sp. girafa, from Ar. zurafa, zarafa.

girasol.etymology: It. girasole, or F. girasol, fr. L. gyrare to turn around + sol sun.

girdle.etymology: OE. gurdel, girdel, AS. gyrdel, fr. gyrdan; akin to D. gordel, G. gürtel, Icel. gyr. See Gird, v. t., to encircle, and cf. Girth, n.

girl.etymology: OE. girle, gerle, gurle, a girl (in sense 1): cf. LG. gör child.

girth.etymology: Icel. gjör girdle, or ger girth; akin to Goth. gaírda girdle. See Gird to girt, and cf. Girdle, n.

gist.etymology: OF. giste abode, lodgings, F. gîte, fr. gésir to lie, L. jac, prop., to be thrown, hence, to lie, fr. jacre to throw. In the second sense fr. OF. gist, F. gît, 3d pers. sing. ind. of gésir to lie, used in a proverb, F., c'est là que gît le lièvre, it is there that the hare lies, i. e., that is the point, the difficulty. See Jet a shooting forth, and cf. Agist, Joist, n., Gest a stage in traveling.

gittern.etymology: OE. giterne, OF. guiterne, ultimately from same source as E. guitar. See Guitar, and cf. Cittern.

give.etymology: OE. given, yiven, yeven, AS. gifan, giefan; akin to D. geven, OS. g, OHG. geban, Icel. gefa, Sw. gifva, Dan. give, Goth. giban. Cf. Gift, n.

gizzard.etymology: F. gésier, L. gigeria, pl., the cooked entrails of poultry. Cf. Gigerium.

glabella.etymology: NL., fr. L. glabellus hairless, fr. glaber bald.

glace.etymology: F., p.p. of glacer to freeze, to ice. Cf. Glacier.

glacial.etymology: L. glacialis, from glacies ice: cf. F. glacial.

glaciate.etymology: L. glaciatus, p. p. of glaciare to freeze, fr. glacies ice.

glacier.etymology: F. glacier, fr. glace ice, L. glacies.

glad.etymology: AS. glæd bright, glad; akin to D. glad smooth, G. glatt, OHG. glat smooth, shining, Icel. gla glad, bright, Dan. & Sw. glad glad, Lith. glodas smooth, and prob. to L. glaber, and E. glide. Cf. Glabrous.

glade.etymology: Prob. of Scand. origin, and akin to glad, a.; cf. also W. golead, goleuad, a lighting, illumination, fr. goleu light, clear, bright, goleu fwlch glade, lit., a light or clear defile.

gladiator.etymology: L., fr. gladius sword. See Glaive.

glamour.etymology: Scot. glamour, glamer; cf. Icel. glámeggdr one who is troubled with the glaucoma; or Icel. glam-s weakness of sight, glamour; glamr name of the moon, also of a ghost + s sight akin to E. see. Perh., however, a corruption of E. gramarye.

glance.etymology: Akin to D. glans luster, brightness, G. glanz, Sw. glans, D. glands brightness, glimpse. Cf. Gleen, Glint, Glitter, and Glance a mineral.

gland.etymology: F. glande, L. glans, glandis, acorn; akin to Gr. Parable, n.

glare.etymology: OE. glaren, gloren; cf. AS. glær amber, LG. glaren to glow or burn like coals, D. gloren to glimmer; prob. akin to E. glass.

glass.etymology: OE. glas, gles, AS. glæs; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. glas, Icel. glas, gler, Dan. glar; cf. AS. glær amber, L. glaesum. Cf. Glare, n., Glaze, v. t.

glauconite.etymology: Cf. F. glauconite, glauconie, fr. L. glaucus. See Glaucous.

glaze.etymology: OE. glasen, glazen, fr. glas. See Glass.

gleam.etymology: Cf. OE. glem birdlime, glue, phlegm, and E. englaimed.

glebe.etymology: F. glèbe, L. gleba, glaeba, clod, land, soil.

gleet.etymology: OE. glette, glet, glat, mucus, pus, filth, OF. glete.

glen.etymology: Of Celtic origin; cf. W. glyn a deep valley, Ir. & Gael. gleann valley, glen.

glib.etymology: Prob. fr. D. glibberen, glippen, to slide, glibberig, glipperig, glib, slippery.

glide.etymology: AS. glidan; akin to D. glijden, OHG. glitan, G. gleiten, Sw. glida, Dan. glide, and prob. to E. glad.

glimmer.etymology: Akin to G. glimmer a faint, trembling light, mica, glimmern to glimmer, glimmen to shine faintly, glow, Sw. glimma, Dan. glimre, D. glimmen, glimpen. See Gleam a ray, and cf. Glimpse.

glimpse.etymology: For glimse, from the root of glimmer.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

glissando.etymology: As if It. = Fr. glissant sliding.

glisten.etymology: OE. glistnian, akin to glisnen, glisien, AS. glisian, glisnian, akin to E. glitter. See Glitter, v. i., and cf. Glister, v. i.

glister.etymology: OE. glistren; akin to G. glistern,glinstern, D. glinsteren, and E. glisten. See Glisten.

glitter.etymology: OE. gliteren; akin to Sw. glittra, Icel. glitra, glita, AS. glitenian, OS. glitan, OHG. glizzan, G. gleissen, Goth. glitmunjan, and also to E. glint, glisten, and prob. glance, gleam.

gloat.etymology: Akin to Icel. glotta to smile scornfully, G. glotzen to gloat.

globe.etymology: L. globus, perh. akin to L. glomus a ball of yarn, and E. clump, golf: cf. F. globe.

globigerina.etymology: NL., fr. L. globus a round body + gerere to bear.

globule.etymology: L. globulus, dim. of globus globe: cf. F. globule.

glomerulus.etymology: NL., dim. of L. glomus. See 3d Glome.

gloom.etymology: AS. glom twilight, from the root of E. glow. See Glow, and cf. Glum, Gloam.

glorification.etymology: L. glorificatio: cf. F. glorification. See Glorify.

glorify.etymology: F. glorifier, L. glorificare; gloria glory + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

gloriole.etymology: L. gloriola a small glory, dim. of gloria glory.

gloriosa.etymology: Nl., fr. L. gloriosus. See Glorious.

glorious.etymology: OF. glorios, glorious, F. glorieux, fr. L. gloriosus. See Glory, n.

glory.etymology: OE. glorie, OF. glorie, gloire, F. gloire, fr. L. gloria; prob. akin to Gr. glory, praise, to hear. See Loud.

gloss.etymology: Cf. Icel. glossi a blaze, glys finery, MHG. glosen to glow, G. glosten to glimmer; perh. akin to E. glass.

glossary.etymology: L. glossarium, fr. glossa: cf. F. glossaire. See 3d Gloss.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

glottis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. Gloss an explanatory remark.

glove.etymology: OE. glove, glofe, AS. gl; akin to Icel. gl, cf. Goth. l palm of the hand, Icel. l.

glow.etymology: AS. gl; akin to D. gloeijen, OHG. gluoen, G. glühen, Icel. gl, Dan. gloende glowing. Gloom.

glue.etymology: F. glu, L. glus, akin to gluten, from gluere to draw together. Cf. Gluten.

glume.etymology: L. gluma hull, husk, fr. glubere to bark or peel: cf. F. glume or gloume.

glut.etymology: OE. glotten, fr. OF. glotir, gloutir, L. glutire, gluttire; cf. Gr. gar. Cf. Gluttion, Englut.

gluten.etymology: L., glue: cf. F. gluten. See Glue.

glutinous.etymology: L. glutinosus, fr. gluten glue: cf. F. glutineux. See Gluten.

glutton.etymology: OE. glotoun, glotun, F. glouton, fr. L. gluto, glutto. See Glut.

glycerin.etymology: F. glycérine, fr. Gr. glykero`s, glyky`s, sweet. Cf. Glucose, Licorice.

glycerine.etymology: F. glycérine, fr. Gr. glykero`s, glyky`s, sweet. Cf. Glucose, Licorice.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.
A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

glyph.etymology: Gr. glyphe. Cf. Cleave to split.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

gnarl.etymology: From older gnar, prob. of imitative origin; cf. G. knarren, knurren. D. knorren, Sw. knorra, Dan. knurre.

gnash.etymology: OE. gnasten, gnaisten, cf. Icel. gnastan a gnashing, gn to gnash, Dan.knaske, Sw. gnissla, D. knarsen, G. knirschen.

gnaw.etymology: OE. gnawen, AS. gnagan; akin to D. knagen, OHG. gnagan, nagan, G. nagen, Icel. & Sw. gnaga, Dan. gnave, nage. Cf. Nag to tease.

gnome.etymology: F. gnome, prob. fr. Gr. i. e., of the treasures in the inner parts of the earth, or fr. Know.

gnostic.etymology: L. gnosticus, Gr. gignw`skein to know: cf. F. gnostique. See Know.

gnu.etymology: Hottentot gnu, or nju: cf. F. gnou.

goad.etymology: AS. gad; perh. akin to AS. gar a dart, and E. gore. See Gore, v. t.

goal.etymology: F. gaule pole, Prov. F. waule, of German origin; cf. Fries. walu staff, stick, rod, Goth. walus, Icel. völr a round stick; prob. akin to E. wale.

goat.etymology: OE goot, got, gat, AS. gat; akin to D. geit, OHG. geiz, G. geiss, Icel. geit, Sw. get, Dan. ged, Goth. gaits, L. haedus a young goat, kid.

goblet.etymology: F. gobelet, LL. gobeletus, gobellus; cf. L. cupa tub, cask. See Cupel.

goblin.etymology: OE. gobelin, F. gobelin, LL. gobelinus, fr. Gr. kobold, E. kobold, cobalt, Armor. gobilin an ignis fatuus, goblin.

goby.etymology: F. gobie, L. gobius, gobio, Gr. Gudgeon.

god.etymology: AS. god; akin to OS. & D. god, OHG. got, G. gott, Icel. gu, go, Sw. & Dan. gud, Goth. gup, prob. orig. a p. p. from a root appearing in Skr. h, p. p. h, to call upon, invoke, implore. Goodbye, Gospel, Gossip.

godhead.etymology: OE. godhed. See -head, and cf. Godhood.

roots.meaning: A variant of -hood.
A suffix forming adjectives and adverbs, and denoting likeness or resemblance.

godwit.etymology: Prob. from AS. g good + wiht creature, wight.

goggle.etymology: Cf. Ir. & Gael. gog a nod, slight motion.

goiter.etymology: F. goître, L. guttur throat, cf. tumidum guttur goiter, gutturosus goitered. See Guttural.

goitre.etymology: F. goître, L. guttur throat, cf. tumidum guttur goiter, gutturosus goitered. See Guttural.

gold.etymology: AS. gold; akin to D. goud, OS. & G. gold, Icel. gull, Sw. & Dan. guld, Goth. gulp, Russ. & OSlav. zlato; prob. akin to E. yellow. Yellow, and cf. Gild, v. t.

golden.etymology: OE. golden; cf. OE. gulden, AS. gylden, from gold. See Gold, and cf. Guilder.

goldfinch.etymology: AS. goldfinc. See Gold, and Finch.

golding.etymology: From the golden color of the blossoms.

golf.etymology: D. kolf club or bat, also a Dutch game played in an inclosed area with clubs and balls; akin to G. kolben club, but end, Icel. k tongue of a bell. bolt, Sw. kolf bolt, dart, but end, Dan. kolv bolt, arrow. Cf. Club, Globe.

goliard.etymology: From OF. goliart glutton, buffoon, riotous student, Goliard, LL. goliardus, prob. fr. L. gula throat. Cf. Gules.

gondola.etymology: It., dim. of gonda a gondola; cf. LL. gandeia a kind of boat, Gr. gondole gondola, cup.

gong.etymology: AS. gong, gang, a going, passage, drain. See Gang.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

good.etymology: AS. God, akin to D. goed, OS. god, OHG. guot, G. gut, Icel. goedhr, Sw. & Dan. god, Goth. gods; prob. orig., fitting, belonging together, and akin to E. gather. sq. root29 Cf. Gather.

goodly.etymology: OE. godlich, AS. g. See Good, and Like.

goosander.etymology: OE. gossander, a tautological word formed fr. goose + gander. Cf. Merganser.

goose.etymology: OE. gos, AS. g, pl. g; akin to D. & G. gans, Icel. gas, Dan. gaas, Sw. g, Russ. guse. OIr. geiss, L. anser, for hanser, Gr. hamsa. sq. root233. Cf. Gander, Gannet, Ganza, Gosling.

gooseberry.etymology: Corrupted for groseberry or groiseberry, fr. OF. groisele, F. groseille, -- of German origin; cf. G. krausbeere, kräuselbeere (fr. kraus crisp), D. kruisbes, kruisbezie (as if crossberry, fr. kruis cross; for kroesbes, kroesbezie, fr. kroes crisp), Sw. krusbär (fr. krus, krusing, crisp). The first part of the word is perh. akin to E. curl. Cf. Grossular, a.

gopher.etymology: F. gaufre waffle, honeycomb. See Gauffer.

gore.etymology: AS. gor dirt, dung; akin to Icel. gor, SW. gorr, OHG. gor, and perh. to E. cord, chord, and yarn; cf. Icel. görn, garnir, guts.

gorge.etymology: F. gorge, LL. gorgia, throat, narrow pass, and gorga abyss, whirlpool, prob. fr. L. gurgea whirlpool, gulf, abyss; cf. Skr. gargara whirlpool, gr to devour. Cf. Gorget.

gorgeous.etymology: OF. gorgias beautiful, glorious, vain, luxurious; cf. OF. gorgias ruff, neck handkerchief, and F. gorge throat, and se pengorger to assume airs. Cf. Gorge, n.

gorget.etymology: OF. gorgete, dim. of gorge throat. See Gorge, n.

gorilla.etymology: An African word; found in a Greek translation of a treatise in Punic by Hanno, a Carthaginian.

gorse.etymology: OE. & AS. gorst; perh. akin to E. grow, grass.

goshawk.etymology: AS. g, lit., goosehawk; or Icel. gashaukr. See Goose, and Hawk the bird.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

gospel.etymology: OE. gospel, godspel, AS. godspell; god God + spell story, tale. See God, and Spell, v.

gossamer.etymology: OE. gossomer, gossummer, gosesomer, perh. for goose summer, from its downy appearance, or perh. for God's summer, cf. G. mariengarr gossamer, properly Mary's yarn, in allusion to the Virgin Mary. Perhaps the E. word alluded to a legend that the gossamer was the remnant of the Virgin Mary's winding sheet, which dropped from her when she was taken up to heaven. For the use of summer in the sense of film or threads, cf. G. Mädchensommer, Altweibersommer, fliegender Sommer, all meaning, gossamer.

gossip.etymology: OE. gossib, godsib, a relation or sponsor in baptism, a relation by a religious obligation, AS. godsibb, fr. god + sib alliance, relation; akin to G. sippe, Goth. sibja, and also to Skr. sabha assembly.

gouge.etymology: F. gouge. LL. gubia, guvia, gulbia, gulvia, gulvium; cf. Bisc. gubia bow, gubioa throat.

gourd.etymology: F. gourde, OF. cougourde, gouhourde, fr. L. cucurbita gourd (cf. NPr. cougourdo); perh. akin to corbin basket, E. corb. Cf. Cucurbite.

gout.etymology: F. goutte a drop, the gout, the disease being considered as a defluxion, fr. L. gutta drop.

govern.etymology: OF. governer, F. gouverner, fr. L. gubernare to steer, pilot, govern, Gr. Gubernatorial.

government.etymology: From Middle English governement , from Old French governement (modern French gouvernement ), from governer (see govern ) + -ment . Morphologically govern +‎ -ment . Displaced native Old English gerec , leodweard , ræden , rǣding and ealdordōm .

governor.etymology: OE. governor, governour, OF. governeor, F. gouverneur, fr. L. gubernator steersman, ruler, governor. See Govern.

gown.etymology: OE. goune, prob. from W. gwn gown, loose robe, akin to Ir. gunn, Gael. gùn; cf. OF. gone, prob. of the same origin.

grab.etymology: Ar. & Hind. ghur crow, raven, a kind of Arab ship.

grace.etymology: F. grâce, L. gratia, from gratus beloved, dear, agreeable; perh. akin to Gr. hary to desire, and E. yearn. Cf. Grateful, Gratis.

gracious.etymology: F. gracieux, L. gratiosus. See Grace.

gradation.etymology: L. gradatio: cf. F. gradation. See Grade.

grade.etymology: F. grade, L. gradus step, pace, grade, from gradi to step, go. Cf. Congress, Degree, Gradus.

gradient.etymology: L. gradiens, p. pr. of gradi to step, to go. See Grade.

gradual.etymology: Cf; F. graduel. See Grade, and cf. Gradual, n.

graduate.etymology: Cf. F. graduer. See Graduate, n., Grade.

graduation.etymology: LL. graduatio promotion to a degree: cf. F. graduation division into degrees.

roots.meaning: A final syllable signifying a ruler, as in landgrave, margrave. See Margrave.

graft.etymology: OE. graff, F. greffe, originally the same word as OF. grafe pencil, L. graphium, Gr. carve. So named from the resemblance of a scion or shoot to a pointed pencil. Cf. Graphic, Grammar.

grail.etymology: OF. greel, LL. gradale. See Gradual, n.

grain.etymology: F. grain, L. granum, grain, seed, small kernel, small particle. See Corn, and cf. Garner, n., Garnet, Gram the chick- pea, Granule, Kernel.

gram.etymology: AS. gram; akin to E. grim. sq. root35.

grammar.etymology: OE. gramere, OF. gramaire, F. grammaire Prob. fr. L. gramatica Gr Gramme, Graphic, and cf. Grammatical, Gramarye.

grammatical.etymology: L. grammaticus, grammaticalis; Gr. grammatical. See Grammar.

gramme.etymology: F. gramme, from Gr. that which is written, a letter, a small weight, fr. to write. See Graphic.

gramophone.etymology: Gr. a thing drawn or written (fr. write) + - phone, as in telephone.

grampus.etymology: Probably corrupted from It. gran pesce great fish, or Sp. gran pez, or Pg. gran peixe, all fr. L. grandis piscis. See Grand, and Fish. the animal.

granadilla.etymology: Sp., dim. of granada pomegranate. See Grenade, Garnet.

granary.etymology: L. granarium, fr. granum grain. See Garner.

grand.etymology: OE. grant, grount, OF. grant, F. grand, fr. L. grandis; perh. akin to gravis heavy, E. grave, a. Cf. Grandee.

grandiloquent.etymology: L. grandis grand + logui to speak.

grandiose.etymology: F. grandiose, It. grandioso. See Grand.

grange.etymology: F. grange barn, LL. granea, from L. granum grain. See Grain a kernel.

granite.etymology: It. granito granite, adj., grainy, p. p. of granire to make grainy, fr. L. granum grain; cf. F. granit. See Grain.

grant.etymology: OE. graunten, granten, OF. graanter, craanter, creanter, to promise, yield, LL. creantare to promise, assure, for (assumed LL.) credentare to make believe, fr. L. credens, p. pr. of credere to believe. See Creed, Credit.

granule.etymology: L. granulum, dim. of granum grain: cf. F. granule. See Grain a kernel.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

grape.etymology: OF. grape, crape, bunch or cluster of grapes, F. grappe, akin to F. grappin grapnel, hook; fr. OHG. chrapfo hook, G. krapfen, akin to E. cramp. The sense seems to have come from the idea of clutching. Cf. Agraffe, Cramp, Grapnel, Grapple.

graphic.etymology: L. graphicus, Gr. graphique. See Graft.

graphical.etymology: L. graphicus, Gr. graphique. See Graft.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

grapnel.etymology: OE. grapenel, dim. fr. F. grappin the grapple of a ship; of German origin. See Grape.

grapple.etymology: F. grappiller, OF. graypil the grapple of a ship, fr. graper to pluck, prop., to seize, clutch; of German origin. See Grape.

grasp.etymology: OE. graspen; prob. akin to LG. grupsen, or to E. grope. Cf. Grab, Grope.

grass.etymology: OE. gras, gres, gers, AS, qr, g; akin to OFries. gres, gers, OS., D., G., Icel., & Goth. gras, Dan. gr, Sw. gr, and prob. to Z. grcen, grow. Cf. Graze.

grate.etymology: L. gratus agreeable, grateful: cf. It. & Sp. grato. See Grace, and cf. Agree.

grateful.etymology: Grate, a. + full; cf. F. gré thanks, good will, fr. L. gratum, neut. of gratus agreeable, grateful. See Grate, a.

gratify.etymology: F. gratifier, L. gratificari; gratus pleasing + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

gratis.etymology: L., contr. fr. gratiis out of favor or kindness, without recompense, for nothing, fr. gratia favor. See Grace.

gratitude.etymology: F. gratitude, LL. gratitudo, from gratus agreeable, grateful. See Grate, a.

gratuitous.etymology: L. gratuitus, from gratus pleasing. See Grate, a., Gratis.

grave.etymology: F., fr. L. gravis heavy; cf. It. & Sp. grave heavy, grave. See Grief.

gravel.etymology: OF. gravele, akin to F. grve a sandy shore, strand; of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. grouan gravel, W. gro coarse gravel, pebbles, and Skr. gravan stone.

gravid.etymology: L. gravidus, fr. gravis heavy, loaded. See Grave, a.

gravimeter.etymology: L. gravis heavy + -meter: cf. F. gravimètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

gravity.etymology: L. gravitas, fr. gravis heavy; cf. F. gravité. See Grave, a., Grief.

gravy.etymology: OE. greavie; prob. fr. greaves, graves, the sediment of melted tallow. See Greaves.

gray.etymology: OE. gray, grey, AS. grg, grg; akin to D. graauw OHG. gro, G. grau, Dan. graa, Dw. gr, Icel. grdr.

graze.etymology: imp. & p. p. Grazed (p. pr. & vb. n. Grazing.

grease.etymology: OE. grese, grece, F. graisse; akin to gras fat, greasy, fr. LL. grassus thick, fat, gross, L. crassus. Cf. Crass.

great.etymology: OE. gret, great, AS. gret; akin to OS. & LG. grt, D. groot, OHG. grz, G. gross. Cf. Groat the coin.

greaves.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. grevar greaves, LG. greven, G. griebe, also AS. greofa pot. Cf. Gravy.

grebe.etymology: F. grbe, fr. Armor. krib comb; akin to kriben crest, W. crib comb, crest. So called in allusion to the crest of one species.

greed.etymology: Akin to Goth. grdus hunger, Icel. graedhr. sq. root34. See Greedy.

greedy.etymology: OE. gredi, AS. grdig, grdig; akin to D. gretig, OS. grdag, OHG. grtag, Dan. graadig, OSw. gradig, grdig, Icel. graugr, Goth. grdags greedy, grdn to be hungry; cf. Skr. grdh to be greedy. Cf. Greed.

greek.etymology: AS. grec, L. Graecus, Gr. : cf. F. grec. Cf. Grecian.

green.etymology: OE. grene, AS. grne; akin to D. groen, OS. grni, OHG. gruoni, G. grn, Dan. & Sw. grn, Icel. grnn; fr. the root of E. grow. See Grow.

greet.etymology: OE. greten, AS. grtan, grlan; akin to Icel. grata, Sw. gita, Dan. grde, Goth. grctan; cf. Skr. hrd to sound, roar. sq. root50.

gregarine.etymology: NL., fr. Gregarina the typical genus, fr. L. gregarius. See Gregarious.

gregarious.etymology: L. gregarius, fr. grex, gregis, herd; cf. Gr. jar to approach. Cf. Congregate, Egregious.

gregorian.etymology: NL. Gregorianus, fr. Gregorius Gregory, Gr. grégorien.

grenade.etymology: F. grenade a pomegranate, a grenade, or Sp. granada; orig., filled with seeds. So called from the resemblanse of its shape to a pomegranate. See Carnet, Grain a kernel, and cf. Pomegranate.

greyhound.etymology: OE. graihund, greihound, greahund, grihond, Icel. greyhundr; grey greyhound + hundr dog; cf. AS. grghund. The origin of the first syllable is unknown.

griddle.etymology: OE. gredil, gredl, gridel, of Celtic origin; cf. W. greidell, Ir. greideal, greideil, griddle, gridiron, greadaim I burn, scorch. Cf. Gridiron.

gridiron.etymology: OE. gredire, gredirne, from tthe same source as E. griddle, but the ending wass confused with E. iron. See Griddle.

grief.etymology: OE. grief, gref, OF. grief, gref, F. grief, L. gravis heavy; akin to Gr. , Skr. guru, Goth. karus. Cf. Barometer, Grave, a., Grieve, Gooroo.

grievance.etymology: OF. grcvance. See Grieve, v. t.

grieve.etymology: AS. ger. Cf. Reeve an officer.

grievous.etymology: OF. grevous, grevos, LL. gravosus. See Grief.

grill.etymology: F. gril. See Grill, v. t.

grimace.etymology: F., prob. of Teutonic origin; cf. AS. gr mask, specter, Ical. gr mask, hood, perh. akin to E. grin.

grime.etymology: Cf. Dan. grim, griim, lampblack, soot, grime, Icel. gr mask, sort of hood, OD. grijmsel, grimsel, soot, smut, and E. grimace.

grind.etymology: AS. grindan; perh. akin to L. frendere to gnash, grind. Cf. Grist.

grindelia.etymology: NL. Named after D. H. Grindel, a Russian.

grip.etymology: L. gryps, gryphus. See Griffin, Grype.

gris.etymology: OF. & F., fr. LL. griseus; of German origin; cf. MHG. gris, G. greis, hoary. Cf. Grizzle.

grisly.etymology: OE, grisly, grislich, AS. grislic, gryslic, fr. gro shudder; cf. OD. grijselick horrible, OHG. grisenlch, and also AS. gresan to frighten, and E. gruesome.

grison.etymology: F., fr. grison gray, gray-haired, gris gray. See Gris.

grist.etymology: AS. grist, fr. grindan. See Grind.

gristle.etymology: OE. gristel, gristil, AS. gristl; akin to OFries. gristel, grestel. Perh. a dim. of grist but cf. OHG. krustila, krostela. Cf. Grist.

grit.etymology: OE, greet, greot, sand, gravel, AS. greót grit, sant, dust; akin to OS griott, OFries. gret gravel, OHG. grioz, G. griess, Icel. grjot, and to E. groats, grout. See Groats, Grout, and cf. Grail gravel.

grizzle.etymology: F. gris: cf. grisaille hair partly gray, fr. gris gray. See Gris, and cf. Grisaille.

groan.etymology: OE. gronen, granen, granien, AS. gr, fr. the root of grennian to grin. *35. See 2d Grin, and cf. Grunt.

groat.etymology: LG. grote, orig., great, that is, a great piece of coin, larger than other coins in former use. See Great.

groats.etymology: OE. grot, AS. gratan; akin to Icel. grautr porridge, and to E. gritt, grout. See Grout.

grocer.etymology: Formerly written grosser, orig., one who sells by the gross, or deals by wholesale, fr. F. grossier, marchand grossier, fr. gros large, great. See Gross.

grog.etymology: So named fronm "Old Grog" a nickmname given to Admiral Vernon, in allusion to his wearing a grogram cloak in foul weather. He is said to have been the first to dilute the rum of the sailors (about 1745).

grogram.etymology: OF. gros-grain, lit., gros-grain, of a coarse texture. See Gross, and Grain a kernel, and cf. Grog.

groin.etymology: F. groin, fr. grogner to grunt, L. grunnire.

grommet.etymology: F. gourmette curb, curb chain, fr. gourmer to curb, thump, beat; cf. Armor. gromm a curb, gromma to curb.

gromwell.etymology: Called also gromel, grommel, graymill, and gray millet, all prob. fr. F. grmil, cf. W. cromandi.

groom.etymology: Cf. Scot. grome, groyme, grume, gome, guym, man, lover, OD. grom boy, youth; perh. the r is an insertion as in E. bridegroom, and the word is the same as AS. guma man. See Bridegroom.

groove.etymology: D. groef, groeve; akin to E. grove. See Grove.

grope.etymology: OE. gropen, gropien, grapien, AS. gr to touch, grope, fr. gr to gripe. See Gripe.

gross.etymology: F. gros, L. grossus, perh. fr. L. crassus thick, dense, fat, E. crass, cf. Skr. grathita tied together, wound up, hardened. Cf. Engross, Grocer, Grogram.

grot.etymology: F. grotte, It. grotta. See Grotto.

grotesque.etymology: F., fr. It. grottesco, fr. grotta grotto. See Grotto.

grotto.etymology: Formerly grotta, fr. It. grotta, LL. grupta, fr. L. crypta a con cealed subterranran passage vault, cavern, Gr. Grot, Crypt.

ground.etymology: OE. ground, grund, AS. grund; akin to D. grond, OS., G., Sw., & Dan. grund, Icel. grunnr bottom, Goth. grundus (in composition); perh. orig. meaning, dust, gravel, and if so perh. akin to E. grind.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

groundsel.etymology: OE. grundswilie, AS. gpundeswylige, grundeswelge, earlier gundiswilge; gund matter, pus + swelgan to swallow. So named as being good for a running from the eye. See Swallow, v.

group.etymology: F groupe, It. gruppo, groppo, cluster, bunch, packet, group; of G. origin: cf. G. krepf craw, crop, tumor, bunch. See Crop, n.

grouper.etymology: Corrupted fr. Pg. garupa crupper. Cf. Garbupa.

grouse.etymology: Prob. after the analogy of mouse, mice, fr. the earlier grice, OF. griesche meor hen: cf. F. piegrièche shrike.

grout.etymology: AS. grut; akin to grytt, G. grütze, griess, Icel. grautr, Lith. grudas corn, kernel, and Z. groats.

grovel.etymology: From OE. grovelinge, grufelinge, adv., on the face, prone, which was misunderstood as a p. pr.; cf. OE. gruf, groff, in the same sense; of Scand. origin, cf. Icel. grufa, in a grufu on the face, prone, grufa to grovel.

grow.etymology: AS. grawan; akin to D. groeijen, Icel. groa, Dan. groe, Sw. gro. Cf. Green, Grass.

growl.etymology: D. grollen to grunt, murmur, be angry; akin to G. grollen to be angry.

grub.etymology: OE. grubbin., cf. E. grab, grope.

grudge.etymology: OE. grutchen, gruchen, grochen, to murmur, grumble, OF. grochier, grouchier, grocier, groucier; cf. Icel. krytja to murmur, krutr a murmur, or E. grunt.

gruel.etymology: OF. gruel, F. gruau; of German origin; cf. OHG. gruzzi groats, G. grütze, As. grut. See Grout.

gruff.etymology: D. grof; akin to G. grob, OHG. gerob, grob, Dan. grov, Sw. grof, perh. akin to AS. rcófan to break, Z. reavc, rupture, g- standing for the AS. prefix ge-, Goth. ga-.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.

grumble.etymology: Cf. LG. grummeln, grumman, D. grommelen, grommen, and F. grommeler, of German origin; cf. W. grwm, murmur, grumble, surly. sq. root35. Cf. Grum, Grim.

grume.etymology: OF. grume, cf. F. grumeau a little heap, clot of blood, dim. fr. L. grumus.

grunt.etymology: OE. grunten; akin to As. grunian, G. grunzen, Dan. grynte, Sw. grymta; all prob. of imitative; or perh. akin to E. groan.

guacharo.etymology: Cf. Sp. guácharo sickly, dropsical, guacharaca a sort of bird.

guaiacum.etymology: NL., fr. Sp. guayaco, from native name in Hayti.

guanaco.etymology: Sp. guanaco, Peruv. huanacu. Cf. Huanaco.

guano.etymology: Sp. guano, fr. Peruv. huanu dung.

guarantee.etymology: For guaranty, prob. influenced by words like assignee, lessee, etc. See Guaranty, and cf. Warrantee.

guaranty.etymology: OF. guarantie, garantie, F. garantie, OF. guarantir, garantir, to warrant, to guaranty, E. garantir, fr. OF. guarant, garant, a warranter, F. garant; of German origin, and from the same word as warranty. See Warrant, and cf. Warranty, Guarantee.

guard.etymology: OF. guarder, garder, warder, F. garder, fr. OHG. wart to be on the watch, await, G. marten. See Ward, v. & n., and cf. Guard, n.

guardant.etymology: OF. guardant, p. pr. of guard. See Guard, v. t.

guardian.etymology: OF. guardain, gardien, F. gardien, LL. guardianus. See Guard, v. t., and cf. Wasden.

guava.etymology: Sp. guayaba the guava fruit, guayabo the guava tree; prob. fr. the native West Indian name.

gudgeon.etymology: OE. gojon, F. goujon, from L. gobio, or gob, Gr. 1st Goby.

guerdon.etymology: OF. guerdon, guerredon, LL. widerdonum (influenced by L. donum gift, cf. Donation ), fr. OHG. widarl; widar again, against (G. wider wieder) + lon reward, G. lohn, akin to AS. leán Goth. laun. See Withers.

guerrilla.etymology: Sp., lit., a little war, skirmish, dim. of guerra war, fr. OHG. werra discord, strife. See War.

guess.etymology: OE. gessen; akin to Dan. gisse, Sw. gissa, Icel. gizha, D. gissen: cf. Dan. giette to guess, Icel. geta to get, to guess. Probably originally, to try to get, and akin to E. get. See Get.

guest.etymology: OE. gest, AS. gæst, gest; akin to OS., D., & G. gust, Icel gestr, Sw. gäst, Dan. Gjäst, Goth. gast, Russ. goste, and to L. hostis enemy, stranger; the meaning stranger is the older one, but the root is unknown. Cf. Host an army, Hostile.

guide.etymology: OE. guiden, gyden, F. guiaer, It. guidare; prob. of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. ritan to watch over, give heed to, Icel. viti signal, AS. witan to know. The word prob. meant, to indicate, point to, and hence, to show the way. Cf. Wit, Guy a rope, Gye.

guild.etymology: OE. gilds, AS. gild, gield, geld, tribute, a society or company where payment was made for its charge and support, fr. AS. gildan, gieldan, to pay. See Yield, v. t.

guilder.etymology: D. gulden, orig., golden. Cf. Golden.

guile.etymology: OE. guile, gile, OF. guile; of German origin, and the same word as E. wile. See Wile.

guilloche.etymology: F. guillochis; -- said to be fr. Guillot, the inventor of a machine for carving it.

guillotine.etymology: F., from Guillotin, a French physician, who proposed, in the Constituent Assembly of 1789, to abolish decapitation with the ax or sword. The instrument was invented by Dr. Antoine Louis, and was called at first Louison or Louisette. Similar machines, however, were known earlier.

guilt.etymology: OE. gilt, gult, AS. gylt, crime; probably originally signifying, the fine or mulct paid for an offence, and afterward the offense itself, and akin to AS. gieldan to pay, E. yield. See Yield, v. t.

guise.etymology: OE. guise, gise, way, manner, F. guise, fr. OHG. wisa, G. weise. See Wise, n.

guitar.etymology: F. guitare; cf. Pr., Sp., & Pg.guitarra, It. chitarra; all fr. Gr. cithara. Cf. Cittern, Gittern.

gulch.etymology: OE. gulchen; cf. dial. Sw. gölka to gulch, D. gulzig greedy, or E. gulp.

gull.etymology: Prob. fr. gull the bird; but cf. OSw. gylla to deceive, D. kullen, and E. cullibility.

gullet.etymology: OE. golet, OF. Goulet, dim. of gole, goule, throat, F. gueule, L. gula; perh. akin to Skr. gula, G. kenle; cf. F. goulet the neck of a bottle, goulotte channel gutter. Cf. Gules, Gully.

gulp.etymology: D. gulpen, cf. OD. golpe gulf.

gum.etymology: OE. gomme, gumme, F. gomme, L. gummi and commis, fr. Gr. kam; cf. It. gomma.

gumma.etymology: NL. So called from its gummy contents See Gum.

gummite.etymology: So called because it occurs in rounded or flattened pieces which look like gum.

gumption.etymology: OE. gom, gome, attention; akin to AS. geómian, gyman, to regard, observe, gyme care, OS. gomean to heed, Goth. gaumjan to see, notice.

gun.etymology: OE. gonne, gunne; of uncertain origin; cf. Ir., Gael.) A LL. gunna, W. gum; possibly (like cannon) fr. L. canna reed, tube; or abbreviated fr. OF. mangonnel, E. mangonel, a machine for hurling stones.

gunny.etymology: Hind. gon, gon,, a sack, sacking.

gunwale.etymology: Gun + wale. So named because the upper guns were pointed from it.

gurgle.etymology: Cf. It. gorgogliare to gargle, bubble up, fr. L. gurgulio gullet. Cf. Gargle, Gorge.

gurnard.etymology: OF. gornal, gournal, gornart, perh. akin to F. grogner to grunt; cf. Ir. guirnead gurnard.

guru.etymology: Hind. gur a spiritual parent or teacher, Skr. guru heavy, noble, venerable, teacher. Cf. Grief.

gush.etymology: OE. guschen, cf. Icel. gusa and gjsa, also D. gucsen; perh. akin to AS. geótan to pour, G. giessen, Goth. giutan, E. gut. Cf. Found to cast.

gusset.etymology: F. gousset armpit, fob, gusset, dim. of gousse pod, husk; cf. It. guscio shell, or W. cwysed gore, gusset.

gust.etymology: Icel. gustr a cool breeze. Cf. Gush.

gusto.etymology: It. or Sp., fr. L. gustus; akin to E. choose. Cf. 2d GUST, GOUR.

gut.etymology: OE. gut, got, AS. gut, prob. orig., a channel, and akin to geótan to pour. See FOUND to cast.

gutter.etymology: OE. gotere, OF. goutiere, F. gouttière, fr. OF. gote, goute, drop, F. goutte, fr. L. gutta.

guttural.etymology: L. guttur throat: cf. F. gutural.

guy.etymology: Sp. guia guide, a guy or small rope used on board of ships to keep weighty things in their places; of Teutonic origin, and the same word as E. guide. See Guide, and cf. Gye.

guzzle.etymology: OP. gosillier, prob. orig., to pass through the throat; akin to F. gosier throat; cf. It. gozzo a bird's crop.

gymnastic.etymology: L. gymnasticus, Gr. gymnastique. See Gymnasium.

gymnospermous.etymology: Gr. gymno`spermos; gymno`s naked + spe`rma seed: cf. F. gymnosperme.

gynecocracy.etymology: Gr. gynh`, gynaiko`s, a woman + gynécocratie. Cf. Gynocracy.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

gypsum.etymology: L. gypsum, Gr. jibs plaster, mortar, Per. jabs lime.

gypsy.etymology: OE. Gypcyan, F. gyptien Egyptian, gypsy, L. Aegyptius. See Egyptian.

gyrate.etymology: L. gyratus made in a circular form, p. p. of gyrare.

gyre.etymology: Cf. OF. gyrer, girer. See Gyrate.

gyrfalcon.etymology: OE. gerfaucon, OF. gerfaucon, LL. gyrofalco, perh. fr. L. gyrus circle + falco falcon, and named from its circling flight; or cf. E. gier-eagle. See Gyre, n., Falcon.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.
